title: Ono no Komachi's 'Hana no iro wa', Kokinshu 113; Hyakunin isshu 9
greek: 花の色は 移りにけりな いたづらに わが身世にふる ながめせしまに
short: A tanka by Ono no Komachi, in William N. Porter's 1909 translation of the Hyakunin isshu ('One Hundred Poets, One Poem Each').
body: Ono no Komachi (fl. mid-ninth century) is the most famous woman poet of early Heian Japan and one of the 'Six Poetic Immortals' (rokkasen) named in the preface to the Kokinshu (c. 905), the first imperial anthology, where this poem appears as no. 113 among the spring poems. Fujiwara no Teika later chose it as poem 9 of his Hyakunin isshu (c. 1235). The Japanese is a tanka (waka) of thirty-one syllables in five lines (5-7-5-7-7): Hana no iro wa / utsuri ni keri na / itazura ni / waga mi yo ni furu / nagame seshi ma ni. Porter's Victorian version rhymes and adds phrases; his note gives her dates as 834-880, which are traditional and uncertain.

title: hana no iro: the colour of the flowers
short: In Heian poetry 'flowers' (hana) usually means cherry blossoms; 'colour' (iro) also means beauty, charm and love.
body: 花の色 hana no iro, 'the colour of the flowers'. In the Kokinshu period, hana by itself normally refers to the cherry, whose brief bloom was the supreme emblem of transient beauty. 色 iro means colour, but also outward beauty, sensual charm and amorous love, so 'the flower's colour' is from the start also the poet's attractiveness. Porter's 'tint' is accurate to the literal sense; his 'My charms' in l. 3 makes explicit the second meaning that the Japanese keeps within one word.

title: utsuri ni keri na: 'has faded, alas'
short: Utsuru means to fade or change; Porter's 'washed away' anticipates the rain of the next line.
body: 移りにけりな utsuri ni keri na, 'has faded, ah!'. 移る utsuru means 'to change, shift, fade' (of colour), and the auxiliary keri marks sudden realisation, with na an exclamation: 'I see now it has faded!'. Porter's 'is washed away' gives a cause, the rain, that in the Japanese comes later through wordplay. Utsuru also suggests the fickleness of love, as in Komachi's other famous poem on the 'flower of the heart' that fades unseen (Kokinshu 797).

title: pivot-words (kakekotoba): furu and nagame
greek: ふる (降る / 経る); ながめ (長雨 / 眺め)
short: Two puns carry the double meaning: furu is 'to rain' and 'to pass time, age'; nagame is 'long rain' and 'brooding gaze'.
body: The last two Japanese lines, waga mi yo ni furu / nagame seshi ma ni, read in two ways at once. 経る furu, 'to pass (through life), grow old', puns on 降る furu, 'to fall' (of rain); 眺め nagame, 'gazing, brooding, lost in thought', puns on 長雨 nagame, 'long rains' of spring. So the lines mean both 'while I passed my life in the world, lost in vain brooding' and 'while the long rains fell'. Such pivot-words (kakekotoba) are central to Heian technique. Porter's note recognises the double reading. He separates the senses, giving 'heavy showers of rain' to the flowers and 'on the wane' to the woman, rather than fusing them.

anchor: which once I prized so much
title: the poet's fading beauty
short: The speaker's own beauty, like the blossom, has faded; Porter adds 'which once I prized so much', which is not in the Japanese.
body: わが身 waga mi, 'my self, my body', is the human counterpart of the flower. The Japanese does not say that she prized her charms; Porter adds the phrase, perhaps to fit a legend of Komachi's pride. Later tradition, especially Nō plays such as Sotoba Komachi, made her a proud beauty who rejected lovers and ended as a ragged old woman, and Porter's note mentions her 'unhappy old age'. The poem itself, read in the Kokinshu as a spring poem, concerns the regret of time passing while one is absorbed in thought, which modern scholars prefer to read without the biographical legend.

title: 'on the wane'
short: Porter's idiom, from the waning moon, introduces an English image of decline not present in the Japanese.
body: 'On the wane' (OED: in a state of decline, originally of the moon) is Porter's English cliché for decline, supplying a rhyme with 'rain' and 'vain'. The Japanese has no corresponding phrase: the decline is implied by furu, 'to grow old in the world'. Porter's version makes the parallel between flower and woman explicit with 'also', where Komachi's lines let the two meanings overlap.

title: itazura ni: 'in vain, to no purpose'
short: Itazura ni ('in vain, idly') sits at the centre of the Japanese poem and can attach to either half; Porter moves it to the end.
body: いたづらに itazura ni, the third line of the Japanese, means 'uselessly, in vain, idly'. Placed in the middle, it can modify the fading of the flowers (they faded without being enjoyed) or the passing of the poet's life (spent in vain brooding), and it hinges the two halves of the poem. Porter's note says the middle line applies to both flower and beauty. His final line, 'Both bloomed, alas! in vain', moves the word to the end and adds 'bloomed' and 'alas', turning reticent regret into an explicit lament. The added fifth rhyming line is his way of imitating the tanka's five-line shape.

title: Ki no Tsurayuki's judgement of Komachi
short: The Kokinshu preface praised Komachi's poems as moving but 'not strong', like a lady who is ill: a judgement that shaped her reputation.
body: In the Japanese preface (Kana jo) to the Kokinshu, Ki no Tsurayuki described Komachi as belonging to the line of the ancient Princess Sotoori: her poetry was full of feeling but lacked strength, like a beautiful noblewoman suffering from illness. The comparison, partly praise and partly criticism, made her the model of passionate, melancholy women's poetry. Her other poems in the Kokinshu are largely love poems about dreams and longing. Porter's note also records a legend that her verse ended a drought in 866, an example of the belief that great poetry can move heaven and earth, stated in the same preface.
